name: Worship of Fortune and belief in astrological Fate
plain_explanation: With life made unpredictable by constant war, palace revolutions, and economic instability, people turned either to worshipping 'Fortune' (blind luck) or to astrology, which promised that the future, however grim, was at least fixed and knowable in advance.
precise_definition: Two complementary popular responses to Hellenistic insecurity: the cult of Tyche (Fortune/Luck) as an arbitrary power governing events, and the Chaldean/Babylonian doctrine of astrological determinism, which most people (and even most philosophers) held simultaneously without noticing the inconsistency.
why_it_mattered: Marks, for Russell, the point at which Greek rationalism began to be swamped by 'oriental' superstition, a process that continued until the triumph of Christianity.
historical_origin: Astrology reached the Greek world through Alexander's opening of contact with Babylon; Russell cites the Chaldean Berosus, who taught astrology at Cos.
examples: The Chaldean priest Berosus teaching astrology at Cos
Royal tombs (Ozymandias, Antiochus I) decorated with astrological symbols
influence_on_later_thinkers: Astrology persists as a serious intellectual temptation for later Stoic philosophers (Ch. XXVIII) and other Hellenistic thinkers.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly religious; Russell treats it as the chief 'bad' side of the meeting of Greek and 'barbarian' cultures.
